title: Marian's assessment of Jimmy as a musician
summary: Marian praises his sound and describes her broadening.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x:
When I started this interview some hours ago, I said that I thought that I was one of the luckiest of the interviewers. And now I'm convinced that I am. Because in addition to the wonderful hours I have spent with you, Jimmy, we now have Marian with us. (LAUGHTER).

And although we have talked about Marian I just think I'll let Marian talk a little bit for herself. (LAUGHTER). And I think a rather sensible question and one that you can answer honestly even sitting close to him, has to do with your assessment of him as a musician. Not as a husband, as a musician. (LAUGHTER).

I was going to say, either way Helen we need about three days more. But I'll try to sum up as quickly as I can.

I think from the first time that I heard Jimmy play I was always tremendously impressed with the sound

the individual sound that he had. And some of my best memories of his playing are when we first started together when he was in the Army and I was with the USO and listening to him play standard tunes, like 'Embracable You' and things that we would play for the troops you know.

And always with this little individual twist. Something different and special and even though Jimmy kind of, oh, what shall I say, identifies himself to a great extent with Bix Beiderbecke, who was indeed an idol of Jimmy's. Still and all I think that though he does have a little, maybe a little touch or a little sound of Bix in his playing that he's too modest actually about the individual and special sound that he gets, you know.

He has a very strong, driving kind of a forceful sound and it's very much, it's very much a part of his personality. I think people play the way they are, you know. In fact I always used to say to Jimmy and I still do, like I would send him an opening night card or telegram and I would say, play some merry notes. And that's how they would come out a lot of times. (LAUGHTER).
Just kidding. That puts Marian in a terrible spot to you know, come out and say something.

No, at this point in your lives she can be honest (I believe) I said that you know. Yes, because I think that if something was up and something was down Marian would mention the down. But really I think, no, in all seriousness and I'm not putting you on now, the overall assessment simply has to be one that is full of praise. There's no question about that, about Your musicianship.

I must say this Helen. Years ago when I first started playing with my trio, I feel as if I probably wasn't as well rounded a musician as I am now. I'm not making jokes, like Jimmy's always saying I'm well rounded and he's talking about my figure. (LAUGHTER).
But what I meant was musically more broadminded. There was a period in my life when I think that I thought of older music, traditional, more traditional music.

Well classical jazz, whatever you want to call it. I didn't enjoy playing it quite as much as I do now. I think I've gone full circle. I've been a part of playing the progressive jazz, sort of delved a little bit into free jazz and avant garde, and I can come back to playing tunes like 'Royal Garden Blues' and all the tunes that Louis played and all the good old tunes.
And I think I can play them with more enjoyment and more zest than I did years ago.
